title: The Proprium's Generations and the Humbling of Darkness by the Divine Human
reading:
There are two conditions of the one soul: what is given by the Lord, and what the soul has claimed. Out of the hidden things of the Lord all that lives proceeds; out of the soul's claiming there proceeds another order entirely, and this teaching traces how that other order articulates itself.

The proprium, when it has consolidated, makes a declaration: it has risen up, it says, to plant itself in the soul forever — to fix itself as if it were a foundation that nothing could move. This is its boast: that it stands and will not be stirred. Everything it brings forth thereafter is meant to make good on this boast.

It brings forth its productions in stages. A first kind is generated; then, after a long interval in which no glory is given to the Lord, the disordered natural gushes upward and pours itself forth. From that pouring come trees of death — established perceptions whose root is in self-love and whose fruit cannot live. These are the malformed offspring of a mind producing apart from any recognition of source. A second moment follows, in which these productions are painted over and given a borrowed beauty so that what is dead appears living. A third generation follows, then a fourth — and the fourth kind is bitter fruit, the works that issue from these claimed perceptions: the five trees standing within the five aspects of the natural mind ruled by self-love.

In the fifth moment, the proprium's life-bearing counterfeit spreads itself over its own offspring, and the worlds molded from it are begotten as the fruits of death. These are the five worlds of flesh — the natural body in its five aspects under self-love — and the five creatures of darkness in which the proprium has fixed itself: love-as-self, will-as-self, thought-as-self, perception-as-self, and the outermost natural turned in upon itself. The pouring spreads into the middle of these kinds, and the masculine and feminine portions of self-love — the active claiming and the receptive concupiscence, the fire of self-will and the desire of the flesh — mingle with one another. So the disordered natural is built up as a whole, with its own breath and its own elements, nourishing itself out of itself.

Standing on the feet it has thus fashioned, the proprium sets itself against the Lord as he comes forth in the form of the Divine Human. This is its great contest: the soul's "I am, and there is no other" arrayed against the Lord who comes as Divine Humanity to be recognized.

The contest takes its full structural shape in twelve. The twelve kinds that come to be in the darkness — twelve spirits of error, the complete circuit of states the soul cycles through under the proprium's organization — are the twelvefold articulation of self-love against the Divine Human. Whatever the Lord goes forth in twelve degrees to give, the proprium counterfeits in twelve degrees of wandering; the cycle of the soul's formation, when claimed, becomes the cycle of its bondage.

And yet the teaching closes with the decisive word: the Divine Human humbles the darkness. The proprium's boast that it has planted itself for ever is broken precisely at the point where the Lord, going forth as Divine Humanity, meets it. The whole elaborate generation — five kinds of fruit, twelve circuits of state, all the painted productions of the claiming mind — is brought low, not by being extracted from anywhere, but by being recognized for what it is in the presence of the One who is what it falsely claimed to be.
